article.headline: North America's Fertilizer Colossus Has a Sulfur Problem
article.lede: When a geopolitical shock closes the Strait of Hormuz to fertilizer trade, the intuitive beneficiary is the dominant North American producer insulated from Gulf supply chains. The Mosaic Company (MOS) fits that description on potash — but not on phosphate, where it is simultaneously a price beneficiary and a cost victim. The contradiction explains why a company posting $12.4 billion in trailing revenue is trading near five-year lows at a $7.2 billion market cap.
article.body:
The Strait of Hormuz crisis of 2026 is no ordinary commodity shock. Since military strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026 effectively closed the waterway, roughly one-third of global seaborne fertilizer trade has been severed, trapping an estimated 16 million tonnes of annual export capacity. *Urea* — the world's most widely traded nitrogen fertilizer, synthesized from natural gas — surged between 25 and 60 percent depending on the market, with global spot prices reaching roughly $585 per tonne by mid-March, up from approximately $465 before the conflict. Iran, the Gulf's largest urea exporter with roughly 9 million tonnes of annual capacity, is offline. Saudi Arabia's Ma'aden (1211.SR) has managed only a handful of phosphate shipments through the Strait since February. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization has warned that scarcity will affect next planting seasons and global food supplies.

The Mosaic Company (MOS) is the dominant phosphate and *potash* producer in North America — claiming 73 percent of the continent's concentrated phosphate production and roughly 40 percent of its potash. The *integrated producer* label means Mosaic mines raw rock and processes it into finished crop nutrients under one corporate roof: it owns nearly 200,000 acres of phosphate-bearing land in Central Florida and runs processing plants in Florida and Louisiana to make *DAP* (diammonium phosphate) and *MAP* (monoammonium phosphate). Its potash comes from four mines in Saskatchewan operated through *Canpotex*, the Canadian potash export cartel, and one mine in Carlsbad, New Mexico. With $12.4 billion in trailing revenue, the company's $7.2 billion market cap implies a price-to-revenue ratio of roughly 0.58 — distressed by historical standards.

On potash, Mosaic (MOS) is fully insulated: its Saskatchewan and New Mexico mines have zero Gulf supply chain exposure. Phosphate is different. Converting phosphate rock into DAP or MAP requires dissolving it in *sulfuric acid*, which demands large quantities of elemental sulfur. Approximately 44 to 45 percent of global seaborne sulfur trade transits the Strait. When the blockage hit, Tampa spot sulfur prices climbed toward $1,200 per tonne. The consequences landed in Mosaic's first-quarter 2026 results: a $373 million operating loss, a $280 million increase in phosphate raw-material costs in a single quarter, production cuts at its Bartow and Louisiana plants to roughly half of *nameplate capacity*, and the withdrawal of all full-year 2026 phosphate guidance. Chief financial officer Luciano Siani Pires told investors: “At $1,200 per ton sulfur price, much, if not all, of the producer cost curve is underwater.” Mosaic is not merely exposed to the Hormuz crisis on phosphate — it is one of its victims.

The potash leg of the thesis remains intact, and it grounds the recovery argument. Canpotex was fully committed through June and on pace for a record year; potash prices rose modestly even as nitrogen prices spiked. Chief executive Bruce Bodine told investors that “there is not going to be enough phosphate to meet global demand” — a bet that once sulfur supply normalizes, Mosaic (MOS) will be first to capture elevated prices with existing processing infrastructure. Sixteen analysts hold an average price target of $32.19, roughly 41 percent above the current price of $22.78; RBC Capital Markets upgraded to Outperform on the thesis that current phosphate margins are unsustainably depressed. The stock's 52-week high of $38.23 shows the market once priced in exactly that recovery — before the Hormuz crisis added a second layer of disruption.

The poster's provocation — that investors cannot eat Nvidia (NVDA) chips — is shorthand for a real valuation argument: that markets have systematically re-rated *AI infrastructure* stocks while commodity producers with irreplaceable roles in food production trade at distressed multiples. The argument has its own blind spot. Mosaic's (MOS) path to re-rating runs through a geopolitical resolution no analyst can schedule. A ceasefire would unlock Gulf sulfur supply, restore Mosaic's cost structure, and simultaneously release the Gulf phosphate exports backed up since February — flooding a market starved of supply. The recovery trade and the overhang arrive together, or not at all.

concepts.definition: A nitrogen-rich synthetic fertilizer produced from natural gas via the Haber-Bosch process. It is the world's most traded nitrogen fertilizer by volume and a benchmark for global fertilizer pricing. Urea prices move closely with natural gas costs and are a leading indicator of food-production input inflation.

A family of potassium-bearing minerals mined and processed for use as crop fertilizer. Potassium is one of the three primary plant macronutrients, critical for disease resistance and yield. The major producing regions are Saskatchewan, Canada and Belarus; Mosaic is among the dominant North American producers.

A concentrated phosphate fertilizer produced by reacting phosphoric acid with ammonia. It is one of the most widely applied crop nutrients globally, typically spread before planting to supply both phosphorus and nitrogen. Mosaic is among the world's largest DAP producers.

A high-analysis phosphate fertilizer closely related to DAP but with a lower nitrogen ratio. It is often preferred on alkaline soils where phosphorus — not nitrogen — is the limiting nutrient. Mosaic produces it alongside DAP at its Florida and Louisiana processing facilities.

The offshore marketing arm jointly owned by The Mosaic Company and Nutrien, the two dominant Canadian potash producers. It pools Saskatchewan potash exports and negotiates benchmark prices with major importers such as China and India, functioning as a legal export cartel under Canadian law.

In mining and materials, a company that controls both the extraction of raw ore and its processing into finished product. For Mosaic, this means owning the phosphate rock mines and the chemical conversion plants that turn the rock into DAP and MAP — as opposed to a trader or blender that purchases inputs from third parties.

The key reagent in phosphate fertilizer production. Phosphate rock is dissolved in sulfuric acid to produce phosphoric acid, which is then reacted with ammonia to make DAP or MAP. Producing sulfuric acid requires large quantities of elemental sulfur, making sulfur a critical and non-substitutable input whose price directly determines phosphate production economics.

The maximum output a plant is designed to produce under normal operating conditions, as specified by its engineering design. Running at 50 percent of nameplate — as Mosaic did at its Florida and Louisiana plants in Q1 2026 — means the facility is operating at half its rated throughput, typically because feedstock costs make full-rate production unprofitable.

A ranking of all producers in a market by their marginal cost of production, from lowest to highest. A producer is said to be “underwater” when the prevailing market price falls below its position on the curve — meaning it costs more to produce than the product fetches. When Mosaic's CFO warned the entire cost curve was underwater, he was signaling that most phosphate producers globally, not just Mosaic, faced uneconomic operating conditions.

The data centers, networking equipment, and specialized chips — primarily GPUs from companies like Nvidia — required to train and run large artificial-intelligence models. The term captures the capital-intensive physical layer beneath AI software. The poster contrasts its elevated market valuation with that of commodity producers whose outputs feed people, arguing markets are mispricing physical necessities relative to compute.

article.fact_check: The tweet describes the Hormuz disruption as “the worst fertilizer supply shock ever,” but the Google AI Overview the poster attached is more careful, calling it “one of the most severe fertilizer supply crises in history.” The 2021–2022 period — when Russian natural gas cutoffs, Ukrainian export disruption, and unilateral producer bans drove urea above $900 per tonne in some markets — is a plausible rival for that label. The tweet's claim that Mosaic is “the largest integrated producer of fertilizer in North America” is accurate specifically for phosphate (73% of North American production) and potash (roughly 40%), but the unmodified word “fertilizer” also covers nitrogen (urea, ammonia), in which Mosaic has no significant production; Nutrien is a larger company by revenue and potash capacity overall. The “up to 60%” urea surge figure is at the high end of reported data: CSIS tracked a 26 percent jump in the first week after the strikes; CNBC reported approximately 50 percent since the start of the conflict; the 60 percent figure appears to reflect specific regional spot markets rather than global benchmarks.

ticker_mos.name: The Mosaic Company
ticker_mos.blurb: The Mosaic Company is one of the world's largest producers and marketers of concentrated phosphate and potash crop nutrients, serving the global agricultural inputs market. It operates through three segments—Phosphates, Potash, and Mosaic Fertilizantes—and owns mines and production facilities that produce diammonium phosphate (DAP), monoammonium phosphate (MAP), MicroEssentials (a value-added ammoniated phosphate), and phosphate-based animal feed ingredients. With approximately 13,249 employees and trailing twelve-month revenue of roughly $12.4 billion, Mosaic is a foundational supplier to the global fertilizer industry. The company went public in October 2004 and is classified in the Materials sector under Agricultural Inputs.
ticker_mos.recent: Mosaic reported Q1 2026 results on May 11, 2026, posting a net loss and operating loss with adjusted EBITDA declining year-over-year; net income fell approximately 88% on a trailing basis to $45 million. The company withdrew its phosphate segment guidance due to raw material constraints and announced production curtailments with significant charges in Brazil, while the Potash segment was a relative bright spot with increased sales volumes and earnings. For Q2, management guided DAP prices of $760–$780 per tonne and potash sales volumes of 1.9 million tonnes, and trimmed full-year 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $1.25 billion; the stock, which traded near its 52-week low, closed at $22.78 on May 13, 2026 (+1.74%), well below analyst consensus target of $30.13.

ticker_1211-sr.name: Saudi Arabian Mining Company (Maaden)
ticker_1211-sr.blurb: Saudi Arabian Mining Company (Maaden) is the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's national mining champion, founded in 1997 and headquartered in Riyadh. It operates across four business units — Phosphate, Aluminium, Base Metals & New Minerals, and other segments — mining gold, phosphate rock, bauxite, kaolin, magnesite, copper, and zinc. With a market capitalization exceeding 250 billion SAR, Maaden is one of the largest mining and metals companies in the Middle East and sells into markets spanning India, Europe, the Americas, Africa, and the broader GCC.
ticker_1211-sr.recent: Maaden reported Q1 2026 earnings on May 2, 2026, posting EPS of 0.42 SAR on revenue of 8.79 billion SAR. The stock has gained roughly 26% over the past year but pulled back about 7% over the past month, trading near 64 SAR as of May 14, 2026. Full-year trailing net income of 7.43 billion SAR represents a 116% year-over-year increase, reflecting strong commodity pricing and operational leverage.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.
